entries.name: Egyptian Mythology (Duat)
entries.description: A perilous nighttime journey the soul takes alongside the sun god Ra, through twelve gates guarded by serpents and fire. At the Hall of Two Truths, Anubis weighs the heart against the feather of Ma'at — the justified pass on to the Field of Reeds; the heart that fails is devoured by Ammit, and the soul ceases to exist.
entries.primaryDoctrine: To achieve eternal life in the Field of Reeds (Aaru), the soul must successfully navigate the Duat's perils and pass the final judgment—the Weighing of the Heart against the feather of Ma'at.
entries.label: Egyptian Mythology (Duat)

entries.name: Greek Mythology (Hades)
entries.description: A grey, misty realm beneath the earth where Charon ferries souls across the water for the price of a coin, and the dead persist as faint shades of their living selves. Later tradition sorts them: Elysium for the blessed, the Asphodel meadows for the many, Tartarus for the great transgressors.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Death is a grim equalizer where most spirits live as blank shadows, unless they achieve heroic glory for Elysium, or commit unforgivable hubris securing a place in Tartarus.
entries.label: Greek Mythology (Hades)

entries.name: Dante's Purgatorio (Catholic Medieval Vision)
entries.description: Dante's vision of purgatory as a steep terraced mountain in the southern sea, where souls willingly climb through seven cornices — one for each deadly sin — toward the Earthly Paradise at the summit. The suffering purifies rather than punishes, and every soul on the mountain is certain of reaching God.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Souls headed for heaven but carrying the stain of unrepented venial sins must willingly embrace agonizing trials to achieve spiritual purification before entering Paradise.
entries.label: Dante's Purgatorio (Catholic Medieval Vision)

entries.name: Naraka (Buddhist Hell Realms)
entries.description: A vast subterranean system of eight hot and eight cold hells where beings burn off the residue of grave karma under Yama's oversight. No sentence is eternal: when the karmic debt is exhausted — even after ages — the being dies out of hell and is reborn on another turn of the wheel.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Naraka is not a place of divine punishment, but an environment manifested entirely by the individual's negative karma. It is temporary, existing only until that karma is exhausted.
entries.label: Naraka (Buddhist Hell Realms)

entries.name: Norse Mythology (Helheim & Valhalla)
entries.description: The dead are divided by manner of death and divine choice: valkyries carry half the battle-slain to Odin's golden Valhalla to feast and train for Ragnarök, Freyja claims the other half for Fólkvangr, and the rest descend to Hel's grey, quiet realm — with corpse-cold Náströnd reserved for oath-breakers.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Fate is inescapable, but the manner of one's death determines their eternal post: either feast in Valhalla with the Aesir or dwell in the grey mists of Hel.
entries.label: Norse Mythology (Helheim & Valhalla)

entries.name: Aztec Mythology (Mictlān)
entries.description: Destination follows manner of death: warriors and mothers lost in childbirth accompany the sun, the drowned go to Tlālōcān — and most souls walk a four-year, nine-level descent through clashing mountains, obsidian winds, and rivers, guided by a dog, to reach Mictlantecuhtli's still realm of Mictlān.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Souls must endure a four-year odyssey through nine layers of trial to reach the final rest in the tenth level, guided by Xoloitzcuintli dogs.
entries.label: Aztec Mythology (Mictlān)

entries.name: Traditional Ainu Religion
entries.description: A mirrored existence where the human world and the world of the kamuy interact through constant reciprocity — gifts, ritual, and sending ceremonies. The dead continue village life in an inverted land where seasons run opposite, and the boundary stays open in both directions to those who keep the exchange.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Reciprocity as the foundation for ethical standards; humans provide prayer and gifts, while gods provide protection and resources.
entries.label: Traditional Ainu Religion

entries.name: Orphic Astral Metaphysics
entries.description: Initiates buried with gold tablets carried instructions for the world below: refuse the spring of forgetting, drink from the lake of Memory, declare “I am a child of Earth and starry Heaven.” Through initiation and lives of purity the soul escapes the grievous circle of rebirth and rises to dwell among the stars.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Sema (the body) is a tomb; the soul is a spark of divine aether trapped in a cycle of rebirth that can only be broken by purity and knowledge.
entries.label: Orphic Astral Metaphysics

entries.name: Melanesian Cargo Cult
entries.description: A millenarian vision recorded across post-contact Melanesia: the ancestors are not gone but withheld, and one day they return on ships and planes bearing the manufactured abundance the living were denied — overturning the colonial order and ushering in an age of plenty and total equality.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The 'Myth-Dream': acquisition of Western material goods through ritual is the symbolic key to restoring human dignity and ending white supremacy.
entries.label: Melanesian Cargo Cult

entries.name: Islam (Akhira & Barzakh)
entries.description: The soul waits in Barzakh between death and resurrection. On the Day of Judgment, every deed is weighed; each soul crosses As-Sirāt, a bridge thinner than a hair over Jahannam, before entering Jannah’s gardens or falling to the fire.
entries.primaryDoctrine: At death the soul enters Barzakh, an intermediate state where the righteous find peace and the wicked find anxiety. On Yawm al-Qiyāmah (the Day of Judgment) every life is weighed on the Mīzān. Each soul must cross As-Sirāṭ, a bridge finer than a hair and sharper than a sword over Jahannam. The righteous pass swiftly to Jannah — gardens beneath which rivers flow, culminating in the Beatific Vision of God. The wicked fall into Jahannam’s fires, which may purify for later release by divine mercy or, for persistent rejection after clarity, endure eternally.
entries.label: Islam (Akhira & Barzakh)

entries.name: Judaism (Sheol → Olam Ha-Ba)
entries.description: Understated by design. The Hebrew Bible names Sheol — a collective shadowy grave. Rabbinic tradition developed Gehinnom (purification, typically capped at twelve months) and Olam Ha-Ba, the World to Come. Emphasis remains on right action in Olam Ha-Zeh — this world.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Jewish afterlife is intentionally understated and plural. The Hebrew Bible describes Sheol — a shadowy collective grave where all the dead descend. The rabbis of the Mishnah and Talmud developed a richer eschatology: Gehinnom, a temporary place of purification (capped at twelve months for most souls, per Mishnah Eduyot 2:10), and Olam Ha-Ba (the World to Come), sometimes read as a disembodied world of souls and sometimes as the bodily resurrection (T’chiyat ha-Metim) at the Messianic age. The focus remains on this life — Olam Ha-Zeh — and on righteous action (mitzvot).
entries.label: Judaism (Sheol → Olam Ha-Ba)

entries.name: Hinduism (Samsara & Moksha)
entries.description: The ātman passes through countless births across fourteen lokas — worlds heavenly and hellish — according to karma. Every state is temporary; even the gods fall when their merit is spent. The cycle ends only in moksha — the ātman’s recognition of its identity with Brahman, the absolute.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The soul (ātman) is beginningless and indestructible, passing through uncountable lives across fourteen lokas — seven higher worlds including Svarga (heavenly realms) and Brahmaloka, and seven lower including Naraka (hells). Each rebirth is shaped by karma — the moral residue of action. Every state is temporary; even the devas fall when their merit is spent. The cycle ends only when the ātman realizes its identity with Brahman, the absolute ground of all being. This realization is mokṣa — liberation. The Bhagavad Gītā teaches four classical paths: Jñāna (knowledge), Bhakti (devotion), Karma (action without attachment), and Rāja (meditation).
entries.label: Hinduism (Samsara & Moksha)

entries.name: Christianity (Last Things — Heaven, Hell, Judgment)
entries.description: At death, each soul faces particular judgment — the righteous enter the Beatific Vision of God, the impenitent enter separation from God. At the end of the age, the dead are bodily resurrected; Christ returns as judge; and creation is renewed as the New Heaven and New Earth. Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions diverge on details; the core shape is shared.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Christian eschatology holds that at death each soul faces a particular judgment and enters an intermediate state — Heaven (the Beatific Vision of God), Hell (final separation from God), or, in Catholic teaching, Purgatory (temporal purification for those saved but imperfect). At the end of the age, the dead are bodily resurrected; Christ returns; a General Judgment is pronounced; and creation is renewed in the New Heaven and New Earth (Revelation 21). Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant, and evangelical traditions diverge on Purgatory’s existence, the nature of Hell’s duration (eternal vs. conditional immortality), and the intermediate state (soul sleep vs. wakeful presence with Christ). The shared core: resurrection, judgment, and the renewed creation.
entries.label: Christianity (Last Things — Heaven, Hell, Judgment)

entries.name: Jainism (Four Gatis)
entries.description: The soul (jīva) is propelled through four gatis — heavenly (deva), human (manuṣya), animal/plant (tiryañca), and hellish (nāraka) — by karmic matter clinging to it. Liberation (mokṣa) comes through the Three Jewels and ascent through fourteen guṇasthānas to Siddhaloka at the universe’s apex.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Jain cosmology holds that every jīva (soul) is beginningless, conscious, and naturally pure — obscured only by karmic particles accumulated through action, especially violence (hiṃsā). These karmas propel the jīva through the four gatis: deva (celestial realms), manuṣya (human), tiryañca (animal, plant, microbial), and nāraka (seven hells of escalating suffering). Liberation requires ascetic renunciation, ahiṃsā, and progress through fourteen guṇasthānas (stages of spiritual purification). The liberated soul (siddha) rises to Siddhaloka at the apex of the loka (universe), where it abides in perfect knowledge, energy, bliss, and being, eternally. Jainism has no creator god; the cosmos is eternal and self-sustaining.
entries.label: Jainism (Four Gatis)

entries.name: Sikhism (Five Khands → Sach Khand)
entries.description: The soul’s ascent passes through five khands — Dharam, Gian, Saram, Karam, and finally Sach Khand, the realm of truth where the self dissolves into the formless Ik Oaṅkār. Karma shapes the journey; grace (naḍar) opens the final door.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Sikhism teaches that the soul passes through countless life forms, drawn by karma, until human birth offers the opportunity for spiritual realization. Through Naam Simran (remembrance of the divine name), seva (selfless service), and the grace of the Guru, the soul ascends through five khands described in Guru Nānak’s Japji Sāhib: Dharam Khand (the realm of righteous action), Gian Khand (the realm of knowledge), Saram Khand (the realm of spiritual effort and refinement), Karam Khand (the realm of grace, where warrior-saints dwell), and Sach Khand (the realm of truth, where the self merges into Ik Oaṅkār — the one, timeless, self-existent creator).
entries.label: Sikhism (Five Khands → Sach Khand)

entries.name: Taoism (Grotto Heavens & Xian)
entries.description: Within sacred mountains lie the Dongtian — ten major and thirty-six minor Grotto Heavens inhabited by the xian (transcendents). Through inner alchemy (neidan), breath, and harmony with the Tao, the adept transforms into a xian capable of dwelling in these hidden paradises; the unrighteous face Diyu, the Ten Courts of Hell, before rebirth.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Religious Taoism holds that the cosmos is pervaded by the Tao and structured into visible and hidden realms. Within sacred mountains are the Dongtian (洞天, Grotto Heavens), traditionally enumerated in the Tang-era systematization as ten major grotto-paradises and thirty-six minor, accompanied by seventy-two Blessed Grounds (Fudi) — inhabited by xian (仙, transcendents) who have cultivated qi through breathwork, meditation, ritual, dietary discipline, and internal alchemy (neidan, 內丹). At death the hun (ethereal soul) can ascend — attaining xian status through cultivation, or receiving ritual salvation through Lingbao liturgy — while the po (corporeal soul) settles to the grave. For the unrighteous, Diyu (地獄), the Ten Courts of Hell, is administered by Yama and his bureaucratic pantheon; punishments are proportional and terminate in rebirth.
entries.label: Taoism (Grotto Heavens & Xian)

entries.name: Tibetan Buddhism (Six Bardos)
entries.description: The stream of consciousness passes through six bardos — transitional states. The three death bardos (chikhai, chönyid, sidpa) unfold across forty-nine days, during which peaceful and wrathful deities manifest. The Bardo Thödol guides the mindstream toward recognition of its own nature as luminous emptiness — and liberation or rebirth.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Vajrayāna Buddhism, especially in the Nyingma school, teaches six bardos: the bardo of this life, of dream, of meditation, and the three death bardos — the bardo of dying (chikhai), the bardo of luminosity (chönyid), and the bardo of becoming (sidpa). Across the forty-nine days between death and rebirth, the mindstream encounters peaceful and wrathful deities — recognized by the initiated as projections of its own nature, luminous emptiness (dharmakāya). Recognition at any stage brings liberation; failure propels the consciousness toward one of the six realms of rebirth, drawn by karmic imprints. The Bardo Thödol — commonly translated as The Tibetan Book of the Dead, more literally Liberation Through Hearing in the Intermediate State — is read to the dying and the recently dead to guide this passage.
entries.label: Tibetan Buddhism (Six Bardos)

entries.name: Shinto (Yomi no Kuni)
entries.description: Yomi no Kuni, the land of the dead, lies beneath the earth. Not a realm of judgment but of pollution (kegare) — the dead are impure, separated by the Great Stone Izanagi sealed behind him when he fled Yomi. Over time, through ancestral rites, the dead become kami — honored protective presences integrated back into the living community.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Shinto cosmology distinguishes Takamagahara (the high plain of heaven), the human world (ashihara no nakatsukuni), and Yomi no Kuni (the land of the dead). Yomi is dark, subterranean, defiled — reached by a path from Izumo. The foundational myth: Izanami dies in childbirth and descends to Yomi, becoming permanently impure; her husband Izanagi pursues her, sees her rotting form, flees, and seals the boundary at Yomotsu-hirasaka with a great stone. Shinto’s afterlife is therefore not about reward or punishment but about separation and the gradual purification that comes through time and proper rite. The dead, through ancestral veneration (sosen sūhai) and liturgy, transition from impure spirit to honored ancestral kami — protective presences reintegrated into the living community.
entries.label: Shinto (Yomi no Kuni)

entries.name: Zoroastrianism (Chinvat Bridge)
entries.description: Three days after death, the soul reaches the Chinvat Peretum — the Bridge of the Separator. For the righteous, it widens into a welcoming road to the House of Song; for the wicked, it narrows to a razor’s edge, and they fall into the Pit of Druj. At the end of time comes frashokereti — the world’s renovation, molten metal, resurrection, and the universal defeat of the Lie.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Zoroastrianism holds that each soul spends three days near the body before facing individual judgment at the Chinvat Peretum (Bridge of the Separator). There thoughts, words, and deeds are tallied by Mithra, Sraosha, and Rashnu. For the righteous (ashavan), the bridge widens into a paved road met by a beautiful maiden — the personification of one’s own righteous daēnā — who leads them through four ascending realms to Anagra Raocha, the endless light beside Ahura Mazdā. For the wicked (dregvant), the bridge narrows to a razor’s edge; they fall into the Pit of Druj — the House of Lies. At the end of time, a savior (Saoshyant) ushers in frashokereti: a river of molten metal will purify all, the dead will rise in their bodies, the wicked will be cleansed (not eternally damned), and Ahura Mazdā will defeat Angra Mainyu forever. The renewed world will be deathless, ageless, and eternally good.
entries.label: Zoroastrianism (Chinvat Bridge)

entries.name: Yoruba (Orun Rere & Àtúnwá)
entries.description: The emi (breath-soul) returns to Orun, the spirit realm, at death. Orun Rere — the good heaven — welcomes those who lived with iwa pele (gentle character); Orun Apadi, the heaven of broken pots, holds the corrupt until they are purified. Rebirth within the lineage (àtúnwá) is common: ancestors return as grandchildren.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Yoruba cosmology holds that every person is composed of ara (body), emi (breath-soul granted by Olodumare at birth), and ori (the personal destiny-head, chosen in Orun before birth). At death the emi returns to Orun — the spirit realm, opposite aye, the living world. Olodumare, the supreme being, is too transcendent to be directly worshipped; the orisha (deities) — whose number is given in Yoruba tradition by the idiomatic formula 'four hundred plus one,' signifying an open-ended pantheon with always 'one more' — and the egungun (ancestors) mediate. The dead are judged by their iwa (character): Orun Rere, the good heaven, receives those who lived with iwa pele (gentle character), good ori, and proper rites; Orun Apadi, the heaven of broken pots (the hot, dry, potsherd-heaven), holds those whose character was corrupt, until purified. From Orun, many souls return as àtúnwá — reincarnation within the same lineage, often as grandchildren. Divination (Ifá) sustains the ongoing dialogue between aye and Orun.
entries.label: Yoruba (Orun Rere & Àtúnwá)

entries.name: Wicca (Summerland)
entries.description: Between lives, the soul rests in the Summerland — an eternal late-afternoon meadow warmed by the Goddess’s presence. It reviews the life just lived and readies for rebirth. No hell, no external judgment; the Threefold Law echoes, and the wheel turns again.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Wicca — a modern Western religion synthesized from British folk magic, ceremonial ritual, and Gardnerian innovation in the mid-20th century — teaches that the soul is an enduring spark that moves through many incarnations. Between lives, the soul rests in the Summerland, variously pictured as an eternal late-afternoon meadow, a sun-warmed orchard, or a quiet shore, in the presence of the Goddess and the Horned God. There the soul rests, reflects on the life just lived without external judgment, reunites with loved ones, and prepares for the next incarnation. The Threefold Law — that energy sent out returns threefold — functions as a moral principle in this life and, in some readings, shapes the terms of the next. There is no hell, no eternal damnation, no single judge; the Summerland is restful, restorative, and transitional.
entries.label: Wicca (Summerland)

entries.name: Mesopotamian (Kur / Irkalla)
entries.description: All the dead descend — kings and paupers alike — to Kur (Sumerian) or Irkalla (Akkadian), the underworld ruled by Ereshkigal. Dusty and dim; the dead eat dust, drink muddy water, wear feathered garments. No moral judgment, no hope of return. The gift of the dead is memory: offerings from the living sustain them.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The Sumerian-Akkadian afterlife is among humanity’s oldest recorded. All the dead — without distinction of piety, wealth, or heroism — descend to Kur (Sumerian) / Irkalla / Ganzir (Akkadian), a subterranean land of no return. The underworld is dusty and cold; the dead wear feathered garments like birds, eat dust, and drink brackish water. The queen Ereshkigal rules from her lapis palace, served by the gatekeeper Neti and the scribe Geshtinanna. The dead retain a ghostly consciousness (gidim), dependent on offerings of food, water, and remembrance from the living; neglected ghosts wander and haunt. There is no moral judgment — no reward, no damnation; the gods themselves have no power to retrieve the dead (Inanna’s descent illustrates). What endures is the name spoken: the great remembered endure; the forgotten fade. The Epic of Gilgamesh dramatizes this — the king’s failed quest for immortality ends with the acceptance that humans die and that what endures is the city one leaves behind.
entries.label: Mesopotamian (Kur / Irkalla)

entries.name: Lakota Spirit Trail (Wanáǧi Tȟačháŋku)
entries.description: A North American Plains tradition in which the released soul travels the Wanagi Tacanku — the spirit road seen in the sky as the Milky Way — from the living camp toward the camp of the ancestors. At a fork in the road an old woman examines each traveler for the marks given in life; the marked pass on, and the unmarked are turned back to wander the earth.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Many Lakota accounts describe death as a journey of the wanáǧi, or spirit, along a star path toward the ancestors. The emphasis is relational: the dead remain connected to kin, place, memory, and the wider sacred order rather than entering a universal court of reward and punishment.
entries.label: Lakota Spirit Trail (Wanáǧi Tȟačháŋku)

entries.name: Digital Afterlife (Mind Uploading & Memory Systems)
entries.description: A modern secular framework in which continuity after death is engineered rather than revealed: mind uploading and whole-brain emulation, cryonic preservation as a bridge, AI memorial agents trained on a person’s data, and the curated digital estate. Its central dispute is not geography but identity — whether the pattern that persists is the person, a copy, or a monument the living maintain.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The digital afterlife asks whether a person can persist as information: a preserved brain, an uploaded mind, an AI reconstruction trained on personal data, or a simulated self. Its central uncertainty is whether continuity of pattern is continuity of person.
entries.label: Digital Afterlife (Mind Uploading & Memory Systems)

entries.name: Enochian Cosmology (Watchers & Waiting Souls)
entries.description: The Second Temple apocalypse of 1 Enoch maps what earlier scripture left dark: rebel Watchers descend, teach forbidden arts, and are imprisoned awaiting judgment, while Enoch tours a hollow western mountain whose chambers hold the dead — separated by moral condition, some beside a spring of bright water, others in pain — all waiting for the final assize. Its fallen angels, sorted dead, and fiery valley seeded Jewish, Christian, and Islamic afterlife imagination.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The Enochic books portray death as a waiting state inside a larger apocalyptic drama: souls are separated in hidden places, rebellious heavenly beings await punishment, and final judgment will expose the moral architecture of the cosmos.
entries.label: Enochian Cosmology (Watchers & Waiting Souls)

entries.name: Celtic Otherworld (Tír na nÓg)
entries.description: The Celtic Otherworld — Tir na nOg, Mag Mell, the lands beneath the sidhe mounds and across the western sea — is a realm of youth, feasting, and abundance running on its own clock: a night there can be a century here. Reached through mist, mounds, or enchanted voyage rather than by dying, it is less a destination for the dead than a parallel country whose borders sometimes open — and whose returnees age all at once when their feet touch mortal soil.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The Celtic Otherworld is not a moral hell or heaven but an adjacent enchanted realm where time bends, youth persists, and the boundary between living, dead, fairy, and divine powers opens through landscape thresholds.
entries.label: Celtic Otherworld (Tír na nÓg)

entries.name: Maya Mythology (Xibalba)
entries.description: In the K’iche’ Maya Popol Vuh, Xibalba is an underworld court reached by dark rivers and a crossroads that tests travelers before they arrive. Its death lords rule through humiliating trials — houses of darkness, blades, cold, jaguars, and bats — until the Hero Twins outwit every test, rise from their own ashes, and strip the lords of their honored standing, breaking the court’s old claim on the dead.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Xibalba is an underworld of ordeal and cunning rather than a simple moral destination. Souls and heroes descend through rivers, crossroads, and houses of trial where death’s powers test identity, courage, and intelligence.
entries.label: Maya Mythology (Xibalba)

entries.name: Polynesian / Māori Spirit Return (Hawaiki)
entries.description: In Maori tradition the spirit travels the length of the land northward to Te Rerenga Wairua, the leaping place at Cape Reinga, descends by the roots of the ancient pohutukawa, and turns for a last look back before crossing the sea toward Hawaiki, the homeland the ancestors sailed from. Death runs the great migration in reverse: a wayfinding voyage home, with the living lineage as the wake the traveler leaves behind.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Many Māori accounts describe the wairua, or spirit, traveling to the northern departure place, descending by the ancient pōhutukawa, and returning across the ocean to Hawaiki. Death is a return through landscape and genealogy.
entries.label: Polynesian / Māori Spirit Return (Hawaiki)

entries.name: Aboriginal Australian Traditions (Return to Country)
entries.description: Across hundreds of Aboriginal nations, death is widely understood as a return: the spirit goes back to the Country, waterhole, or sky-camp it came from, rejoining the ancestral order laid down in the Dreaming. The living walk it home with smoke, song, and mourning law — and the land itself remains the ancestor, present tense.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The Dreaming — altyerre, tjukurpa, and many other names; the English word is W.E.H. Stanner's gloss — is not a bygone creation era but an everywhen: the ancestral beings walked the land, shaped its features, laid down the Law of kinship and ceremony, and settled into the Country itself, where they remain. A person's spirit derives from Country — many nations associate conception with a specific site where a spirit-child waited — and at death, once mourning law is fulfilled, it returns: to its site, to a sky-camp reached along the Milky Way, or to an island of the dead, by region. Several traditions hold multi-part souls whose parts take different roads. Mourning law does the work of passage: smoking ceremonies cleanse, the names and images of the dead are avoided, and in Arnhem Land the cleaned bones traveled in painted hollow-log coffins. There is no universal ledger of reward and punishment; what death asks is right relation — to kin, to Law, to Country — and what it promises is continuity inside the ancestral order that never left.
entries.label: Aboriginal Australian Traditions (Return to Country)

entries.name: Naturalism (Mortal Oblivion)
entries.description: The oldest rival to every map in this atlas: death as the end of experience. Epicurus taught that where death is, we are not; Lucretius added the mirror of the time before birth. Nothing crosses over — what remains is matter returned to the world, and the difference a life made while it ran.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Philosophical naturalism holds that a human being is a living body and nothing besides, so death — the end of the body's functioning — is the end of the person. Epicurus (341–270 BCE) made the classic case in the Garden at Athens: all good and bad lie in sensation, and death is the privation of sensation, so death is nothing to us. Lucretius pressed the symmetry argument: the eternity before birth harmed no one, and the eternity after death is its twin. The position recurs wherever it is thinkable — the Cārvāka materialists of ancient India, strands of Sadducee teaching, Enlightenment freethinkers, and the secular humanism a growing share of the world now professes. In place of an afterlife it offers finitude as instruction (mortality is what makes time weigh something), material continuity (the body's atoms rejoin the world's cycles), and the afterlives that verifiably exist — memory, works, children, consequences — which run on without a rider. There is no judgment because there is no defendant; the tradition's whole moral force is spent on the one life it holds we get.
entries.label: Naturalism (Mortal Oblivion)

entries.name: Gnosticism (Ascent Through the Archons)
entries.description: The soul is a spark of a higher world, held in matter by a lesser creator and his gate-keeping archons. At death the knower ascends, answering each archon with the words and seals learned in life, shedding the psyche's garments level by level, and rejoins the Pleroma — the fullness it fell from. Ignorance, not sin, is the enemy; gnosis is the road.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The Gnostic movements of the second to fourth centuries — Sethian, Valentinian, and their kin — taught a top-heavy cosmos: the true God, unknowable, unfolds into the Pleroma of aeons; a rupture (in most tellings Sophia's fall) produces the demiurge Yaldabaoth, who fashions the material world and rules it with his archons from the planetary spheres. The human being is threefold — matter, psyche, and a pneumatic spark that predates the world. Salvation is by gnosis: revealed knowledge of the spark's origin, carried down by a revealer who descends hidden through the spheres. At death the soul ascends the same route. Each archon halts and questions it; the knower answers with the names, passwords, and seals learned in life (the First Apocalypse of James preserves the script), sheds a garment of psyche at each level, and passes; the unknowing are turned back toward matter until they learn. Judgment is a knowledge-exam, not a ledger of deeds — and in Valentinian teaching the spiritual carry their salvation by nature, a grace older than their works.
entries.label: Gnosticism (Ascent Through the Archons)

entries.name: Chinese Ancestral Religion (Courts of the Ten Kings)
entries.description: The most administered afterlife on record: the hun and po souls part at death, and the person passes through ten magistrate courts where deeds are read from ledgers and purgations served — while the living file appeals in the currency the courts recognize: offerings, spirit money, and the rites of a filial family. Lady Meng's broth of forgetting waits at the exit before rebirth.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Chinese afterlife religion is a synthesis layered over three millennia. Shang oracle bones (c. 1200 BCE) already show ancestors receiving sacrifice and intervening among the living; Zhou and Han sources develop the two-soul frame — the hun rising, the po remaining with the body — and gather the dead beneath Mount Tai. When Buddhism arrived carrying naraka and karma, and religious Taoism its celestial administration, the systems fused into the underworld codified by the Tang-era Scripture on the Ten Kings: diyu as a government. The dead pass through ten courts, each under a magistrate-king (Yanluo Wang, the naturalized Yama, holds the fifth), where karmic ledgers are audited and purgations served. The living hold standing in the process: offerings, spirit money at Qingming and the Ghost Festival, and transferred merit — Mulian's rescue of his mother is the charter — count as currency the courts recognize. At the end Grandmother Meng serves the broth of forgetting and the soul crosses to rebirth, while in the parallel ancestral frame the tablet on the family altar keeps the person present, fed, and consulted for as long as the line remembers.
entries.label: Chinese Ancestral Religion (Courts of the Ten Kings)

entries.name: Inca (The Three Pachas)
entries.description: The Inca cosmos stacks three worlds: Hanan Pacha above, where the Sun receives the honored dead into warmth and plenty; Kay Pacha, this world; and Ukhu Pacha below, a cold inner country for the wicked. But the great dead never fully left — preserved as mallki, they kept their households, attended festivals, and were fed and consulted as seated members of the family.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Inca teaching, as the colonial chroniclers recorded it, sorted the dead by life and rank: those who lived well — above all the nobility — joined the Sun in Hanan Pacha, a world of warmth and plenty, while the wicked descended to Ukhu Pacha, the cold country inside the earth, to eat stones. The Andean testimony that survives in Quechua, the Huarochirí Manuscript, dwells instead on the road: the soul travels to a far country, crosses a river on a bridge the width of a hair, and is carried over by a black dog that remembers being fed. What set the Inca dead apart was presence. The honored dead were preserved as mallki — seated mummy bundles in fine cloth — who kept palaces, lands, and household staffs, attended festivals, and were fed, dressed, and consulted for as long as their lineage kept its side of ayni, the reciprocity that bound living and dead into one economy.
entries.label: Inca (The Three Pachas)

entries.name: Swedenborg (Heaven and Hell)
entries.description: Emanuel Swedenborg's 1758 report from the other world: the newly dead wake in a middle country within days, met by angels, and nothing is sentenced — the externals worn in life fall away until the ruling love stands exposed, and each spirit migrates freely to the heaven or hell that matches it. Heaven is societies of similar loves, employed in useful work; every angel was once a person.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Heaven and Hell (1758) lays out the afterlife as Swedenborg said he inspected it across decades of waking visits. The person who dies rises in the World of Spirits — a middle state between heaven and hell — within days, and is received by angels. Judgment is disclosure, not court: the externals worn in life fall away until the ruling love, what a person actually loved most, stands exposed; then the spirit goes freely where it belongs, as water finds its level. God casts no one into hell — its inhabitants prefer it there. Heaven is innumerable societies of similar loves which together take the form of one vast human being, the Grand Man; its joy is use, not rest; marriage continues where loves truly join; and every angel and every devil was once a person. The general Last Judgment, he reported, had already occurred — in the world of spirits, in 1757.
entries.label: Swedenborg (Heaven and Hell)

entries.name: Manichaeism (The Return of the Light)
entries.description: Mani taught that every living thing holds particles of stolen Light trapped in Darkness, and that salvation is a salvage operation. At death the Column of Glory lifts the freed light to the moon and sun, which ferry it home. Three roads open at the end of a life: the Elect go straight to the Light, the Hearers return to a body for another attempt, and those who refused go to the darkness. When the last particle is recovered, the cosmos burns and the Last Statue rises from what was saved.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Light and Darkness are two eternal principles, and the cosmos is the apparatus built to extract Light that Darkness swallowed. Every living thing holds some of it. Death opens three roads: the Elect, who kept the full rule, are led up the Column of Glory to the moon (the ship of living water) and the sun (the ship of living fire) and into the Realm of Light; the Hearers, who supported the Elect but lived in the world, return to a body for another attempt; those who spent their lives deepening the mixture go down. Salvation is therefore a salvage operation rather than a pardon — the question at death is whether the Light a person carried gets out. When the last recoverable particle is freed, a centuries-long fire dismantles the cosmos, the remaining Darkness is sealed in a pit with the Light that could not be saved, and the Last Statue rises from everything recovered.
entries.label: Manichaeism (The Return of the Light)

entries.name: Mandaeism (The World of Light)
entries.description: The last surviving Gnostic religion, still practiced by Mandaeans of southern Iraq and Iran and their diaspora. The soul is a stranger here, and death is the return trip. Three days after death it begins an ascent through the maṭarta — watch-stations where it is examined, detained, and cleaned of what it picked up in the world — a passage of some forty-five days that the living assist with the masiqta rite. At the threshold Abatur weighs it. There is no eternal hell: the stations purify rather than condemn.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The soul (nišimta) originates in the World of Light and is a stranger in Tibil, the flawed world made by the demiurge Ptahil. Death is the return journey. The soul waits three days near the body, then ascends through the maṭarta — watch-stations held by detaining powers, where it is examined and stripped of what it accumulated in matter — a passage of roughly forty-five days. The living assist with the masiqta, the rite of raising, which equips and lifts the soul through the stations; funerary practice is therefore precise and essential rather than merely commemorative. At the threshold Abatur weighs the soul on his scales. Crucially, there is no eternal hell: the stations purify rather than condemn, and because the Great Life (Hayyi Rabbi) is merciful, souls are ultimately admitted, the nišimta reuniting with its heavenly counterpart, the dmuta.
entries.label: Mandaeism (The World of Light)

entries.name: Latter-day Saints (Degrees of Glory)
entries.description: Joseph Smith's 1832 vision replaced heaven and hell with a graded architecture in which nearly everyone is saved to some degree of glory. The dead wait in the spirit world — paradise or prison, with missionary work running between them — until the resurrection sorts them into three kingdoms named for the sun, moon, and stars. Only a handful, who knew and refused outright, go to outer darkness. Because the dead can still accept the gospel, the living perform baptisms on their behalf, which is why Latter-day Saints keep the world's largest genealogical archive.
entries.primaryDoctrine: At death the spirit enters the spirit world, divided into paradise and spirit prison; the gospel is preached across that boundary, and those in prison may still accept it. Because ordinances require a body, the living perform proxy baptisms for named ancestors, which the dead remain free to accept or refuse — the doctrinal basis for the church’s genealogical work. At the resurrection all receive bodies and are assigned to one of three kingdoms of glory, compared in Doctrine and Covenants 76 to the sun, moon, and stars: the celestial, for those who received the gospel and its covenants, where God dwells and where exaltation, eternal families, and continued progression apply; the terrestrial, for the honorable who did not receive the fullness; and the telestial, for the wicked, described even so as a glory beyond understanding. Only the sons of perdition — those with full knowledge who turned against it — go to outer darkness.
entries.label: Latter-day Saints (Degrees of Glory)

entries.name: Bahá'í (The Worlds of God)
entries.description: The Bahá'í afterlife has no geography at all. Heaven and hell are not places but conditions — nearness to God and remoteness from God — and the soul, which comes into being at conception and does not return to earth, continues after death to progress through what Bahá'u'lláh calls the worlds of God, forever. The soul's state is compared to a bird released from a cage and to a child born out of the womb: the world it leaves was only the place it grew the faculties it will now need.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The soul is a rational, non-material reality that comes into being at conception, is not bound by the body, and continues after death through what Bahá'u'lláh calls the worlds of God — an endless progression. There is no return to earth: reincarnation is explicitly rejected, as is bodily resurrection, the resurrection language of earlier scriptures being read symbolically. Heaven and hell are not locations but conditions: nearness to God and remoteness from God, beginning in this life and continuing after it. The suffering of the remote soul is the suffering of remoteness itself, and it is not final — progress remains possible after death through divine grace and the prayers of the living, though the opportunity to acquire spiritual qualities belonged to embodied life. The governing analogies are developmental: the bird released from its cage, and the child in the womb growing faculties it can only use once born.
entries.label: Bahá'í (The Worlds of God)

entries.name: Apokatastasis (Universal Restoration)
entries.description: The minority Christian tradition holding that hell is remedial and finite, and that God finally restores every rational creature. Origen argued in third-century Alexandria that punishment is corrective rather than retributive; Gregory of Nyssa held the same hope while abandoning Origen’s speculative machinery. The position was condemned in the sixth century — though scholars still dispute exactly what was condemned and by whose authority — and it has resurfaced in every century since.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Punishment after death is corrective rather than retributive, finite rather than everlasting, and God finally restores every rational creature — the apokatastasis of Acts 3:21 and the "all in all" of 1 Corinthians 15:28. Origen argued from the character of God and from aiōnios as pertaining to an age rather than meaning everlasting, though he presented restoration as inquiry rather than settled doctrine and attached it to speculations — pre-existence of souls, a precosmic fall — that later sank his reputation. Gregory of Nyssa kept the hope and dropped the speculations, holding that evil is finite and therefore exhaustible and that purgation removes evil from the creature rather than removing the creature. Isaac of Nineveh grounded the whole in divine love. Anathemas associated with Constantinople II (553) condemned Origenism, though their canonical status is disputed and Gregory was never condemned; the council names him among the Fathers it follows.
entries.label: Apokatastasis (Universal Restoration)

entries.name: BaKongo (Kalunga and the Turning)
entries.description: In BaKongo thought the cosmos is a circle cut by a line of water. Above the Kalunga line is the world of the living; below it, reversed as in a mirror, the world of the dead. The sun does not stop at sunset — it crosses and goes on shining underneath, and a human life follows the same circuit through four moments: musoni, kala, tukula, luvemba. Death is not an exit but the far quarter of the turn, and the ancestors, the bakulu, remain in working relation with the village that keeps them.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The cosmos is a circle divided by Kalunga, a horizontal line of water: Ku Nseke, the world of the living, above; Ku Mpemba, the world of the dead, below and reversed as in a mirror. The sun does not stop at the horizon — it crosses and continues, so that it is day below while it is night above. A human life runs the same circuit through four moments: musoni (conception, formation in the spirit world and the womb), kala (birth and rising), tukula (maturity and full power), and luvemba (death and setting, the crossing into Mpemba). Death is therefore the far quarter of a turn rather than an exit. The dead become bakulu, ancestors who remain in active relation with their lineage, reachable across the water-line through graves marked with white shells and inverted vessels, through mirrors and water, and through minkisi charged by ritual specialists. Continuity depends on the living maintaining that relation.
entries.label: BaKongo (Kalunga and the Turning)

entries.name: Haitian Vodou (Ginen and Anba Dlo)
entries.description: A person is made of parts, and death takes them apart. The gwo bonanj and ti bonanj are separated from the body in the desounen rite, and the spirit goes anba dlo — under the water — where it waits a year and a day. Then the family performs wete mò nan dlo, taking the dead out of the water, and the spirit is drawn into a govi jar, brought back into the household, and set on the road to Ginen: Africa, the ancestral country beneath the sea. The dead who are served well may in time be raised among the lwa.
entries.primaryDoctrine: A person comprises the body, the gwo bonanj (the animating consciousness, and the part displaced when a lwa mounts a serviteur), the ti bonanj (the personal spark or conscience), and the zetwal (the star holding one’s destiny). At death the desounen rite separates spirit from body. The spirit then goes anba dlo — under the water — and remains there a year and a day. The family is obliged to retrieve it: the wete mò nan dlo rite, an all-night working of drum and song, calls the spirit up and settles it in a govi, a clay jar kept in the sanctuary from which the dead may be consulted and may speak. The spirit is afterward set on the road to Ginen, Africa understood as the ancestral homeland beneath the sea. A spirit well served across generations may be elevated among the lwa. Terminology and sequence vary by house and lineage. The catastrophic outcome is not punishment but capture — a gwo bonanj held as a zombi, prevented from making the journey.
entries.label: Haitian Vodou (Ginen and Anba Dlo)

entries.name: Diné (The Chindi and the Turned Face)
entries.description: The Diné account of death is a refusal of the whole genre. There is no reward, no paradise, and no realm anyone hopes to reach. What matters is the chindi — the residue left behind at the last breath, everything in a person that was out of harmony, which lingers and can sicken the living. The response is avoidance and containment: death outdoors where the chindi disperses, a dwelling abandoned if someone dies inside, the name unspoken. The work is not to secure a destination but to restore hózhó among the living.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Traditional Diné teaching offers no desirable afterlife, no reward or punishment for conduct, and no reunion to hope for. At the last breath the chindi is released: not the whole person but the residue — everything that was out of harmony in them. What was good passes into universal harmony and is not the funeral’s concern; the chindi remains, contaminating and capable of causing ghost sickness, a condition with recognized symptoms requiring ceremonial treatment. Practice is therefore containment: death outdoors or away from the dwelling so the chindi disperses; a hogan in which a death occurred abandoned as a chindi hogan, in older practice with its north wall broken open; the name of the dead left unspoken; swift burial by as few people as possible, followed by purification. The religious stake lies in hózhó — harmony among the living — which the ceremonies exist to restore. This describes documented traditional practice; observance varies widely by family and region, and much of the record comes from outsider ethnography.
entries.label: Diné (The Chindi and the Turned Face)

entries.name: Slavic (Nav and the Bird-Country)
entries.description: Reconstructed from folklore, funerary practice, and language rather than from scripture, the pre-Christian Slavic dead go to Nav — the realm of the dead — while Vyraj or Iriy, the warm country beyond the sea or in the crown of the world tree, is where birds and souls winter. Souls linger forty days; birds carry and announce them; the drowned and the wronged stay behind as navki and rusalki. Grave-feasts kept the dead fed. The tidy three-realm cosmos often presented as Slavic is a twentieth-century invention.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Reconstructed from folklore, funerary practice, and comparative linguistics rather than from scripture, since Christianization from the ninth century destroyed or absorbed the primary material. Nav (Navь, Nawia) is the realm of the dead — a genuinely old term, cognate with Slavic words for corpse. Vyraj, also Iriy, is a warm country beyond the sea or in the crown of the world tree where migratory birds winter, and souls travel there as birds: storks and nightjars in summer, crows and ravens in winter. The soul remains near its home for forty days before departing, the source of the fortieth-day memorial still kept in Slavic Orthodoxy. Grave-feasts such as Radunitsa share food and drink with the dead rather than merely offering it. Veles, god of cattle, oaths, and the wet lowland, is reconstructed as the herdsman of that pasture. Those who died wrongly — drowned, suicides, girls dead before marriage — remain as navki and rusalki at water and field edges. The Prav–Yav–Nav triad widely presented as ancient Slavic cosmology derives from the Book of Veles, a twentieth-century forgery, and belongs to modern Rodnovery rather than to pre-Christian belief.
entries.label: Slavic (Nav and the Bird-Country)

entries.name: Finnic (Tuonela Across the Black River)
entries.description: Tuonela — also Manala — lies across a black river, and Tuoni’s daughter rows the dead over it. What waits is not fire and not reward: the good and the wicked arrive at the same grey place and continue as shadows, sleeping in Tuoni’s beds. Tuonetar meets the newcomer with a drink that takes the living world away. A black swan circles the water. The living stay in contact through lament — the itkuvirsi, sung by women, which guides the dead across and carries messages both ways.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Tuonela, also Manala, is the realm of all the dead, reached by crossing a black river that is sometimes slow and sometimes a burning rapid or whirlpool. Tuoni and Tuonetar rule it; their daughter, Tuonen tytti, ferries the dead across; their son stretches iron nets to prevent return. There is no moral sorting: the good and the wicked arrive at the same grey place, continue as shadows, and sleep in Tuoni’s beds. Tuonetar receives the newcomer with a drink — a beer in the Kalevala — that takes the living world away. The Swan of Tuonela circles the water, its song beautiful and fatal. The living can reach Tuonela through skill and daring rather than death: Väinämöinen goes to retrieve words for a spell and escapes by shapeshifting through the nets; Lemminkäinen is killed at the river and reassembled by his mother with a copper rake. Contact is maintained by the itkuvirsi, Karelian lament poetry sung by women in an allusive register, understood to guide the dead across and to carry messages both ways.
entries.label: Finnic (Tuonela Across the Black River)

entries.name: Etruscan (Charun and the Banquet)
entries.description: The Etruscans painted their tombs as dining rooms. The dead recline at a banquet with the family who went before them, wreathed and served, while at the doorway stands Charun — blue-skinned, hook-nosed, tusked, holding a hammer — and Vanth, winged, carrying a torch and a scroll. There is no weighing and no sentence: the demons are escorts and doorkeepers, not judges. Later tombs darken, and the road to Aita and Phersipnai fills with things that were not there before.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Known almost entirely from painted tombs, since the literature is lost. The dead continue at a banquet with the family who preceded them — reclining, served, wreathed, women alongside men and named with their own lineages. The underworld is ruled by Aita and Phersipnai. At the threshold stand two escorts rather than judges: Charun, blue- or green-fleshed, hook-nosed, animal-eared, sometimes tusked, carrying a heavy mallet whose meaning is disputed (the blow of death, the sealing of the tomb, or the irreversibility of both); and Vanth, winged, bearing a torch to light the road and a scroll on which the fate is already recorded. There is no weighing, no tribunal, and no division of the dead by conduct. From the fourth century BCE the tomb imagery darkens — more demons, more monsters, more journey and less banquet — a shift variously read as Etruscan decline under Rome or as the arrival of Greek underworld imagery.
entries.label: Etruscan (Charun and the Banquet)

entries.name: Plato (The Myth of Er)
entries.description: At the end of the Republic, a soldier named Er dies, lies twelve days on the pyre, and revives to report what he saw. Souls are judged and sent up or down for a thousand years — tenfold repayment either way — then gather at a shaft of light where the spindle of Necessity turns. There the Fates set out lots and lives, and each soul chooses its own next life. Most choose badly, out of habit. Then all drink from the river of Forgetting and are shot out like stars into birth.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Told by Er, a soldier who dies, lies twelve days undecayed, and revives on the pyre to report as a witness forbidden to drink. Souls come to a meadow where judges sit between two openings into the earth and two into the sky; the just go up bearing their judgments in front, the unjust go down bearing theirs behind, and each is repaid tenfold across a thousand years. Returning, they travel to a shaft of light where the spindle of Necessity turns, attended by the Sirens and the three Fates. Lots decide the order of choosing; pattern-lives are laid on the ground; and each soul selects its own next life — the herald declaring that responsibility lies with the chooser and God is blameless. Most choose by habit and badly: the first chooser seizes a tyranny without reading it, while Odysseus, choosing last, deliberately takes an ordinary private life. Each then passes under the throne of Necessity, crosses the plain of Forgetting, drinks from the river Ameles, and is carried to birth like a shooting star.
entries.label: Plato (The Myth of Er)

entries.name: Orthodox Toll-Houses (Telonia)
entries.description: In an account held by many Orthodox Christians and disputed by others, the soul spends three days near the earth, then ascends through the air past a series of toll-houses — telonia — where demons produce the record of a particular sin and the escorting angels answer with the good the soul did. What is not covered is seized. The soul is shown heaven and hell over forty days and receives a provisional verdict awaiting the general resurrection. The Church has never dogmatized it, and prominent hierarchs call it false.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The soul remains near the earth for three days, then ascends through the air escorted by angels, halting at a series of toll-houses (telonia) — commonly around twenty — each staffed by demons holding the record for one class of sin. The demons present the account; the angels answer with the soul’s repentance, its good works, and the prayers of the living. A soul whose account is not covered is seized and carried down. From the ninth to the fortieth day it is shown the dwellings of the righteous and the places of torment, and on the fortieth day receives a provisional verdict — provisional because nothing is settled until the general resurrection and the last judgment. The third-, ninth-, and fortieth-day memorials are understood to assist a soul currently under examination. The status of the teaching is disputed within Orthodoxy: defended from ascetic and liturgical sources by figures such as Ignatius Brianchaninov and Seraphim Rose, and rejected as a late quasi-Gnostic import by others, notably Archbishop Lazar Puhalo. It has never been defined conciliarly and is properly a theologoumenon, not dogma.
entries.label: Orthodox Toll-Houses (Telonia)

entries.name: Conditional Immortality (Soul Sleep)
entries.description: A Protestant minority position, held by Seventh-day Adventists, Jehovah’s Witnesses, Christadelphians and a growing number of evangelical theologians: the soul is not naturally immortal. The dead are unconscious — asleep, knowing nothing — until the resurrection. Immortality is a gift given only to the saved. The wicked are not tormented forever but destroyed: the second death is annihilation. And the reward is not a disembodied heaven but a renewed earth, physical and populated.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The soul is not naturally immortal — the doctrine is held to be a Platonic import rather than a biblical teaching, against texts stating that the dead know nothing and that God alone possesses immortality. Death is therefore cessation, and the New Testament language of sleep is literal: the dead are unconscious, with no interval of waiting, no purgatory, no conscious presence in heaven or hell, and no communication with the living. Subjectively there is no gap between dying and the resurrection. Immortality is a gift conferred only on the saved. The wicked are consequently not tormented forever but destroyed — the second death read as annihilation, with the moral argument that endless torture for finite sin is disproportionate and only follows if an immortal soul is assumed. The reward is bodily and terrestrial: resurrection onto a renewed earth with work and dwelling in it, rather than a disembodied heaven. Held by Seventh-day Adventists, Jehovah’s Witnesses, and Christadelphians, and argued increasingly within mainstream evangelical scholarship.
entries.label: Conditional Immortality (Soul Sleep)

entries.name: Spiritism (Kardec)
entries.description: Allan Kardec organized the seance-room material of 1850s Paris into a system and published it as doctrine. Spirits are immortal, they reincarnate as many times as it takes, and the point of every life is moral progress — never punishment. Between lives comes erraticity, a wandering state in which the spirit reviews what it did and helps plan the next attempt. There is no hell and no eternal damnation; suffering is remedial and self-inflicted. Brazil took it seriously, and it is now a mass religion there.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Spirits are created simple and ignorant, are immortal, and progress morally through repeated incarnation, since embodied life is the school in which progress is made. No spirit is destroyed, condemned, or abandoned, and there is no hell and no eternal damnation. Between incarnations the spirit enters erraticity — a wandering, discarnate state in which it remains in contact with the living world, reviews the life just ended with unusual clarity, and participates in planning the trials of the next one, hardships included, as instruments rather than penalties. Suffering after death is the spirit’s own recognition of what it did and its own attachment to the state it made, lasting exactly as long as it refuses to move; the mechanism is remedial and the exit always open. Communication with the dead through mediums is normal and doctrinally central. Charity is the criterion of everything — "outside charity there is no salvation" — expressed in unpaid consultation, passe, disobsession, and large-scale social work.
entries.label: Spiritism (Kardec)

entries.name: Theosophy (Kama-loka and Devachan)
entries.description: Blavatsky’s system divides the human being into seven principles and death into stages. The body goes; the lower vehicles disintegrate in kama-loka, an astral zone where the desire-nature burns itself out and where, Theosophists argued, seance-room "spirits" are usually only the discarded shell. What survives passes into devachan — a long, blissful, essentially subjective rest in which every unfulfilled aspiration is realized — before the ego returns to another incarnation to continue the work.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The human being comprises seven principles: physical body, vital principle, astral double, kama (desire), manas (mind), buddhi, and atma — the higher three forming the enduring individuality. At death these separate on a schedule. The body decays and the vital principle disperses; what remains sinks into kama-loka, an astral region adjacent to the physical world where the desire-nature exhausts itself, longer and more turbulent for lives dominated by appetite. Theosophy held that mediums usually contact not the departed but the kama-rupa, the discarded desire-shell, which retains memories and mannerisms while decaying — the basis of its long quarrel with Spiritualism. What survives enters devachan: a centuries-long, wholly subjective dream in which every spiritual aspiration of the life is fulfilled, unreachable from outside and unaware of the living, its duration proportional to the spiritual material the life produced. When that is exhausted the ego reincarnates, carrying the karmic account forward.
entries.label: Theosophy (Kama-loka and Devachan)

entries.name: Akan (Asamando and the Nsamanfo)
entries.description: The Akan dead cross water to Asamando, the ancestral country — a shadowed mirror of this one — where an old woman, Amokye, receives them at the bank and takes their beads as the toll. Whether they arrive at all depends on the living: the funeral rites are what get a person through, which is why Akan funerals are the largest events a community holds. Those who arrive and are remembered become nsamanfo, ancestors honoured at blackened stools. The okra, the divine spark, returns to Nyame and often comes back into the same matrilineage.
entries.primaryDoctrine: A person is composed of mogya (blood, from the mother, fixing the matrilineage), sunsum or ntoro (spirit, from the father), and the okra, a divine spark loaned by Nyame that carries a destiny agreed before birth. At death the okra returns to Nyame and characteristically reincarnates within the same matrilineage; the sunsum disperses; and the saman, the ancestor-shade, travels to Asamando — a shadowed mirror of the living world with towns, markets and rank — reached by crossing water. At the bank Amokye receives the dead and takes their beads as a toll, which is why the dead are buried ornamented. The crossing depends on the living: the ayie, the funeral, is what accomplishes it, and a person whose family fails to perform it may not arrive and becomes a restless saman. Those received become nsamanfo, senior members of the lineage still owed report and consultation, honoured at blackened stools with libation. Exclusion from the ancestors, rather than punishment, is the sanction — and an ancestor persists only as long as the living keep naming and feeding them.
entries.label: Akan (Asamando and the Nsamanfo)

entries.name: Haudenosaunee (The Sky World Road)
entries.description: For ten days after a death the spirit is still present, and the community behaves accordingly: the dead are spoken to, given a portion of the food, and formally released at the Ten Day Feast. Then the spirit travels the Milky Way — the Path of Souls — back to the Sky World the first woman fell from, a journey with ordeals along it and strawberries, sweet water and light at the end. The Condolence, performed by the opposite moiety, is directed at the grieving rather than the dead: it lifts the mourner’s mind so the nation can function again.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The world was made when Sky Woman fell from the Sky World and was set down on the turtle’s back, so the dead return upward to where people originally came from. For ten days after death the spirit remains present and is treated as present — addressed directly and given a portion of the food. On the tenth day the Ten Day Feast releases it: food is set aside for the dead, belongings are distributed, and the spirit is formally told to go. It then travels the Milky Way, the Path of Souls, a journey often described as taking about a year and containing ordeals as well as lights, flowers, springs of good water, and wild strawberries — the first fruit and a marker of the road. Separately, the Condolence Ceremony is performed for the bereaved by the opposite moiety, never by their own side: its Requickening Address names and restores the faculties grief disables — clouded eyes, stopped ears, obstructed throat — before a successor is raised to a vacant title, so that the Confederacy does not deliberate with darkened minds.
entries.label: Haudenosaunee (The Sky World Road)

entries.name: Sámi (Saivo Beneath the Mountain)
entries.description: The Sámi dead live in saivo — a world inside the sacred mountains, or beneath the false bottom of certain double-bottomed lakes, entered through a small hole. It is not a reward and not a punishment: the saivo-people keep tents, herd, hunt and fish exactly as here, and families continue. Alongside it lies Jábmiidáibmu, the realm of the death-goddess Jábmiidáhkku, generally reckoned the bleaker option. The noaidi reaches both by drum, and negotiates with the dead on behalf of the living.
entries.primaryDoctrine: The dead live in saivo, an other-world inside the landscape: within the sacred mountains in Norwegian areas, and beneath particular double-bottomed lakes in Finnish ones, entered through a small hole, with such lakes recognized by exceptional clarity and abundant fish. The saivo-people live as they did — pitching tents, herding, hunting, fishing, remaining with their families — so saivo is neither reward nor punishment but the same life continuing out of sight. Certain families held hereditary ties to particular saivo mountains, and a noaidi could inherit saivo helping-spirits in animal form from a predecessor. Alongside it the sources describe Jábmiidáibmu, ruled by the death-goddess Jábmiidáhkku, generally reported as the bleaker destination, with Rota’s disease-realm beyond. The noaidi reached these worlds by frame drum, joik and trance, travelling to negotiate with the dead — illness often being understood as the dead calling a living person, requiring a substitute to be bargained. The record derives largely from Lutheran missionaries engaged in suppressing the practice, and regional variation was considerable.
entries.label: Sámi (Saivo Beneath the Mountain)

entries.name: Cārvāka (Lokāyata)
entries.description: India’s materialist school denied the whole apparatus from inside the Indian conversation: no soul separable from the body, no karma, no rebirth, no heaven, no hell, no liberation. Consciousness arises from the elements as intoxication arises from mixed ingredients, and ends when they disperse. Its most quoted line advises borrowing to drink ghee, since the body once burned does not return. Almost nothing of its literature survives — it is known mostly through opponents quoting it in order to refute it.
entries.primaryDoctrine: Only the four perceptible elements — earth, water, fire and air — are real; ether is rejected as imperceptible. Perception is the sole reliable means of knowledge, and inference is unreliable because it rests on an unverifiable general premise, which is precisely how the other schools reach souls and karma. There is no ātman distinct from the body: consciousness emerges when the elements are combined in a living body, as intoxicating power emerges from ingredients none of which is intoxicating alone, and ceases when the combination ends. There is therefore no rebirth, no karmic carry-forward, no svarga, no naraka, and no mokṣa, since there is no bondage of the kind assumed. Vedic ritual is criticized as an economy benefiting its priests — if the sacrificed animal reaches heaven, why not sacrifice one’s own father? The verse attributed to Bṛhaspati advises living joyfully while life lasts, since the body once burned does not return. The literature survives almost entirely in hostile quotation, chiefly Mādhava’s Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha, so the hedonism may be caricature and the epistemology the serious core.
entries.label: Cārvāka (Lokāyata)
